summary: Defines a portion of the MIB for the Fabric Configuration Server function of a Fibre Channel network, so management tools can read information about it. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Storage networks have a configuration helper. This note defines the standard list of questions a management tool can ask it.

subtitle: The SNMP objects that let a management tool discover a Fibre Channel fabric's switches, ports and platforms.

tldr.problem: A Fibre Channel storage network has a Fabric Configuration Server that knows the fabric's topology, but management applications need a standard way to trigger discovery and read the results over SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The T11-FC-FABRIC-CONFIG-SERVER-MIB module defines managed objects to start a discovery of one or more Fabrics, to read the discovered Interconnect Elements, ports and platforms, and to monitor the server through statistics and notifications.
tldr.outcome: It gives SNMP-based tools a common view of fabric topology. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Fabric Index on a single physical Fabric

today: RFC 4935 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2007. The unit data lists no obsoleting or updating RFC.

sections.title: What the MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 4935 defines a MIB (Management Information Base) module for the Fabric Configuration Server (FCS) function of a Fibre Channel network. The FCS gives a management application a way to discover Fibre Channel fabric topology and attributes.

Discovered topology includes Interconnect Elements (switches, hubs, bridges and so on) with their ports, and "platforms" made of one or more Fibre Channel nodes. The memo was previously approved by INCITS Task Group T11.5 and is a product of the IETF's IMSS working group.

Like other MIB documents, it works inside the Internet-Standard Management Framework: objects are accessed mostly through SNMP and defined with SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580).
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a school with a clipboard that lists every classroom and who sits in it. This document defines the standard way for a manager to read that clipboard from far away.

sections.title: Fibre Channel Terms Used by the MIB
sections.content:
Fibre Channel is logically a bidirectional point-to-point serial data channel. It carries higher-level protocols such as SCSI command sets and IP. Communication points are called N_Ports, joined either by a switching network called a Fabric or by a point-to-point link. A Fabric may consist of several Interconnect Elements, some of which are switches.

An N_Port attaches to a switch port called an F_Port. A switch port linked to another switch by an Inter-Switch Link is an E_Port. Many components have globally unique names, typically World Wide Names (WWNs), and frames carry 24-bit address identifiers whose top level is the Domain_ID.

The FCS is defined in FC-GS and is one of the functions collectively called the Management Service. It can be distributed among switches and accessed from any Nx_Port, though it is not required to be part of a Fabric.
sections.plainLanguage: Every computer and switch in the storage network has a name tag that no one else shares, and an address that the switch hands out. The helper keeps track of all of them.

sections.title: What the Server Knows
sections.content:
The information in each FCS is modeled as a Fabric made of one or more Interconnect Elements, each with some physical ports, plus Fibre Channel nodes grouped into Platforms to make discovery and management easier.

  • An Interconnect Element may have a name, type, Domain Identifier, Management Identifier, Logical Name, management addresses, an information list and a zoning enforcement status.
  • A port may have a name, type, TX type, module type, physical port number, attached port names, state and speed.
  • A platform may have a name, type, description, label, location and management address.

Information about "OS LUN Map Entries", which FC-GS-5 counts as part of a platform, is not in this MIB. It is available from the scsiLunMapGroup in the SCSI MIB (RFC 4455).
sections.plainLanguage: The helper keeps a list of every switch, every plug on each switch, and every group of computers, along with details like names and speeds.

sections.title: Indexes and Relationship to Other MIBs
sections.content:
This MIB builds on the Fibre Channel Management MIB (RFC 4044), which replaced the earlier switch-focused MIB in RFC 2837. It imports common textual conventions from RFC 4439 and RFC 4438.

Three indexes organize the data. The fcmInstanceIndex identifies a Fibre Channel management instance, a separable managed instance of Fibre Channel functionality. The fcmSwitchIndex identifies a switch among those managed by one instance. The Fabric Index (T11FabricIndex) distinguishes Fabrics, and is always 1 when a device is on a single physical Fabric with no virtual Fabrics.

Because a switch may have ports on several Fabrics, fcmSwitchIndex is listed before t11FcsFabricIndex when both appear in an INDEX clause, which simplifies queries about all the Fabrics a switch is connected to.
sections.plainLanguage: Each switch and each separate network gets a number, so a question like "tell me about switch 2 in network 1" has one clear answer.

sections.title: The Six MIB Groups
sections.content:
The module has six groups of objects.

  • t11FcsDiscoveredConfigGroup: the configuration discovered by Fabric Configuration Servers.
  • t11FcsDiscoveryStatusGroup: monitoring the status of discovery.
  • t11FcsDiscoveryControlGroup: requesting an FCS to discover the configuration of one or more Fabrics.
  • t11FcsStatisticsGroup: statistics about the FCS.
  • t11FcsNotificationGroup: three notifications.
  • t11FcsNotificationInfoGroup: control and information objects for the notifications.

The three notifications fire when an FCS rejects a registration, deregistration or query request, when it completes discovery on a range of Fabrics, and when it learns that a management address of an Interconnect Element has changed.
sections.plainLanguage: The questions are sorted into six folders: what was found, how the search is going, a button to start a search, some counts, and alarms with their settings.

sections.title: Why Notifications Are Not Rate-Limited
sections.content:
Notifications for data-plane events normally need flow control, such as a maximum number per interval plus a way to count suppressed ones. The RFC explains why that is not done here: all the notifications in this module come from control-plane events that cannot start a chain reaction.

It also argues that estimating a maximum per unit time is too simplistic. For example, how many t11FcsDiscoveryCompleteNotify notifications can occur depends on the size of the network, how many Virtual Fabrics must be discovered and how quickly an operator can ask for another discovery. The extra complexity is judged not warranted.
sections.plainLanguage: Alarms that only ring when someone asks for a search cannot pile up by themselves, so there is no need for a limit on how often they ring.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Some objects are read-write or read-create. Setting the discovery range, timeout and start objects can trigger a topology discovery, and t11FcsDiscoveryStatus can abort a discovery or invalidate discovered information. The RFC warns that invalidating discovered topology could let an attacker hide unauthorized equipment on the network. The notification enable objects can also be changed.

Readable objects such as the IE, port, platform and statistics tables expose the topology of the Fibre Channel network, so even GET and NOTIFY access should be controlled.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. Implementors are RECOMMENDED to use the SNMPv3 security features, and deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators must configure access so only legitimate principals can read or change the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The map must not be erased or read by strangers. Use the strong lock, SNMPv3, and give keys only to people who need them.
